title: Content and presentations machine
promise: An editorial calendar that actually gets kept: scripts, pieces and decks produced with AI, checked against the brand guide and approved before they see the light of day.
audience: communications, marketing and training leads at small businesses, academies, associations and institutions publishing with one and a half hands
plain: This is building a small newsroom where there used to be one person putting out fires. The problem with institutional content isn't writing one post: it's publishing every week without it showing who had a bad day, having everything sound like the same organization, and making sure nobody publishes an old figure or a promise that can't be kept. This kit solves it with four pieces: an editorial calendar that lives in a sheet and runs everything else; a draft factory where AI turns each calendar row into a script, post or deck outline starting from approved messages (not from its imagination); a brand review with a checklist that catches the odd tone and the invented fact; and a logged approval before anything gets published. Gamma and Canva build the decks and visual pieces from those scripts. The difference from "asking ChatGPT for posts" is the same as between a cook with an organized pantry and one improvising with whatever's on hand: here the AI works with your messages, your data and your approved social proof, and what comes out sounds like you. It works just as well for the academy posting on Instagram and LinkedIn as for the association that needs a decent deck for grant applications.
fits: You publish "when there's time", which means three weeks of nothing followed by four posts in one day
Every sales or institutional deck gets built from scratch the night before, and each one looks like a different company made it
An academy that needs to announce courses, deadlines and results on social media without hiring anyone
A sales team asking for "a presentation for tomorrow" and communications can't keep up
An association presenting reports and projects for grants, always with the deck done at the last minute
A monthly newsletter that dies at issue three from lack of a system, not lack of ideas
The boss wants "to be on LinkedIn" but nobody's decided what to say or to whom
You have good success stories and testimonials nobody's turned into publishable pieces
Everyone writes in their own style and the brand sounds like an out-of-tune choir
Webinars or talks that get prepared well and then aren't reused: one talk should yield ten pieces
notFor: Publishing opinion on sensitive topics (politics, health, vulnerable groups) with AI and without reinforced review: there a tone mistake is a crisis, not a typo
Buying followers overnight: this is a consistency factory, not a virality lever
Press releases and crisis communications: that's handled by a person with judgment and a phone, not a calendar
Publishing on behalf of third parties (clients) without their written approval circuit: their brand, their rules, their signature
When nobody can dedicate even two hours a week: the system reduces the work per piece, it doesn't eliminate it; without those hours the calendar becomes a list of reproaches

scopes.label: Minimum
scopes.what: One channel (whichever works best for you), one piece a week, calendar in a sheet, bank of approved messages, AI drafts and approval via Slack or email before publishing. Manual publishing.
scopes.time: One week part-time, 8-10 hours to set up
scopes.cost: €0-10 a month: free plans and API usage (cents per piece)
scopes.skip: Skip decks, video and reminder automation. One weekly piece that goes out every week already puts you ahead of most.

scopes.label: Standard
scopes.what: Two or three channels with per-channel adaptation, calendar with statuses, connected draft factory (this kit's flow), brand review with checklist, decks with Gamma or Canva from approved scripts, and monthly metrics on what worked.
scopes.cost: €20-60 a month: Gamma or Canva paid plan, n8n and API
scopes.skip: Skip avatar video and the newsletter if it didn't already exist. Every new format is a new factory to maintain.

scopes.label: Advanced
scopes.what: Everything above plus systematic recycling (one talk becomes clips, posts and an article), short video pieces, monthly performance reports by piece type, a social-proof bank with archived consents, and several approvers by content type.
scopes.cost: €60-200 a month depending on video tools and volume
scopes.skip: Don't start here, and don't add video until text has been going out on time for two months: video multiplies production cost by five and forgives half as much.

brief.name: Define the machine before writing a single post
brief.when: First thing. Before opening Canva, before asking for content ideas, before promising leadership anything.
brief.prompt:
Act as a content director experienced with small organizations with no team. We're going to build a content and presentations system, and I want you to force me to define it before producing anything.

My context:
- Organization and what it sells or does: [ORGANIZATION]
- Who we want to reach and what we want them to do: [AUDIENCE AND ACTION]
- What gets published today, where and how often, without dressing it up: [TODAY]
- Who can dedicate hours and how many a week: [HANDS]
- What raw material exists: cases, data, photos, recorded talks, the boss's opinions: [RAW MATERIAL]
- Who has to approve before publishing and how long they take to reply: [APPROVER]
- What's forbidden or sensitive in our sector: [LIMITS]
- Which presentations repeat (sales, institutional, training): [DECKS]

Do this, in this order:

1. Give me my situation back as two lists: what's working in our favor (raw material, channels already working) and what's going to sink us (slow approver, zero hours, no data). Mark with WARNING what you're assuming.
2. Ask me only the three questions that would most change the plan. Stop dead and wait.
3. When I answer, tell me what we should NOT publish: topics where we have nothing to say, formats we can't sustain, channels where our audience isn't. Be restrictive.
4. Propose the minimum sustainable pace: channel, piece type and frequency these specific hands can maintain twelve weeks straight without heroics. Justify the number with the hours I gave you.
5. Write the twelve-week success criterion with observable numbers: pieces published against planned (consistency is the top metric), and one realistic business metric (inquiries received, decks delivered on time), not "engagement".

Don't give me content ideas yet. Don't make me a calendar yet. If you think this plan isn't sustainable with these hours and this approver, tell me with numbers and propose what to cut.

fill.what: Who you are and what you offer, in two lines
fill.example: Civil service exam academy in Murcia, 200 students, in-person and online

fill.what: Who you talk to and what you want them to do
fill.example: Exam candidates aged 22-35 and their parents; get them to book a trial class

fill.what: The truth about what's published now
fill.example: Instagram when someone remembers, last post three weeks ago; a 2023 sales deck

fill.what: Real people and real weekly hours
fill.example: Lucía (coordinator) 3 hours a week, and a teacher who helps sometimes

fill.what: What already exists and can be told
fill.example: 5 years of pass-rate data, 30 testimonials on Google, recorded classes, photos

fill.what: Who signs off and their real speed
fill.example: The director; replies same-day on WhatsApp, within a week by email
Don't promise passing rates, don't use student names without permission, careful comparing academies
Open house deck (twice a year) and dossier for high schools (each term)

brief.expect: The two lists with warnings, three questions, the list of what not to publish, a minimum sustainable pace justified by your hours, and a success criterion with consistency as the main metric.
brief.stuck: If it proposes four channels and daily content, it hasn't used your hours: tell it "with three hours a week, recalculate". And if it asks you to start by making a fancy new brand deck, stop it: pace first, luxuries later.

architecture.what: The document with what the organization can state: key messages, dated facts, social proof with permission, tone and forbidden words.
architecture.nocode: A shared two-to-three-page document, approved by leadership once, reviewed each quarter.
architecture.code: A versioned context file injected into every model call.
architecture.why: It's the factory's pantry. Without it, the AI fills in with plausible-sounding adjectives and facts; with it, every piece starts from statements leadership already signed off. It's approved once and serves a hundred times: it's the piece that saves the most approvals.

architecture.what: The sheet that runs the show: what piece, for which channel, which message from the bank it uses, who's making it, when it goes out and what state it's in.
architecture.nocode: Google Sheets with one row per piece and closed statuses: idea, draft, review, approved, published.
architecture.code: A table with the same fields if the rest of the stack already lives in a database.
architecture.why: The calendar turns "we should publish more" into rows with a date and an owner. And the status turns arguments into information: you can see exactly where each week gets stuck.

architecture.what: The circuit that turns a calendar row into a draft: the AI receives the piece type, the message from the bank and the channel, and returns the text or the script.
architecture.nocode: This kit's n8n flow: every morning reads the calendar, writes what's due and leaves it ready for review.
architecture.code: A script doing the same with prompt templates per piece type.
architecture.why: The automatic draft breaks the blank page, which is where calendars die. The person goes from writing from scratch to fixing something decent, which is three times faster and much more forgiving.

architecture.what: The intermediate step between text and the visual tool: the slide script or the graphic piece's description, approved before laying it out.
architecture.nocode: Gamma generates the deck from the script; Canva builds the pieces with brand templates.
architecture.code: Custom templates that generate pieces from the script.
architecture.why: Laying out before approving the script is the expensive mistake: every content correction costs three times as much on assembled slides. First you approve what's said, then you make it pretty.

architecture.what: The checklist run against every piece: tone, facts against the bank, forbidden words, image rights, and sector-specific sensitivities.
architecture.nocode: A short list in the sheet itself plus an AI pass with this kit's review prompt, which flags problems but doesn't approve.
architecture.code: The same review as an automatic tagging step, with the decision always human.
architecture.why: AI reviews eight pieces fast and without fatigue; the person decides. Separating review (machine, proposes) from approval (person, signs off) gives speed without giving up the wheel.

architecture.what: The logged sign-off from whoever's responsible, followed by publishing on the channel.
architecture.nocode: Slack approval with buttons from the flow; manual or scheduled publishing on the platform.
architecture.code: Publishing via the channel's API only after logged approval.
architecture.why: Nothing goes out without a signature, and the signature is written down. The day a piece causes a problem, you'll know which version went out, who approved it and when: the difference between a mistake and an internal scandal.

architecture.what: Where published pieces live and the habit of reusing them: one talk is ten pieces, one success story is three formats.
architecture.nocode: A folder organized by month and a column in the calendar: "parent piece" each derivative comes from.
architecture.code: The same archive with pieces tagged by topic and format.
architecture.why: The cheapest content is what you already paid for. Organizations don't have an idea problem: they have a problem of not reusing what they already made.

architecture.what: The four figures for each month: pieces planned vs. published, which type worked best, attributable inquiries, and cost.
architecture.nocode: Half an hour a month with each platform's native stats, noted in a tab.
architecture.code: A flow that pulls metrics via API wherever the platform allows it.
architecture.why: Without this, next month's calendar is made by feel. With it, the piece type that's not working gets replaced with data in hand, and consistency (published/planned) gets defended to leadership with a number.

stack.nocode: An HTTP call to the Anthropic API from n8n with the message bank in the prompt.
stack.code: The SDK with prompt templates per piece type.
stack.pick: A medium model with a good prompt beats a big one with a vague prompt. The message bank inside every call is non-negotiable: it's what separates your voice from generic text.

stack.nocode: Gamma from the approved script; exports to PDF and PowerPoint.
stack.code: Custom templates (Marp, slidev) if the team already lives in code.
stack.pick: Gamma for speed with good results. The golden rule comes before the tool: the script gets approved as text before anything gets laid out.

stack.nocode: Canva with brand templates created once and locked: fixed colors, fonts and logo.
stack.code: Custom HTML templates for repetitive pieces if there's technical staff.
stack.pick: Canva plus template discipline. The temptation to "try a different style" on every piece is how the brand dissolves in three weeks.

stack.nocode: Google Sheets: calendar, message bank (or a link to the doc), and metrics tabs.
stack.code: Airtable if you need views by status and channel; same structure.
stack.pick: Sheets until two people start stepping on each other editing. Leadership must be able to open the calendar without asking anyone's permission: transparency is part of the system.

stack.nocode: n8n with this kit's flow: reads the calendar, writes, requests review and logs.
stack.code: A scheduled script doing the same.
stack.pick: n8n: when a piece comes out odd, seeing the run with the prompt and response tells you in a minute whether the problem was the calendar row, the bank or the model.

stack.nocode: Slack with buttons for approval; email if leadership doesn't use Slack.
stack.pick: Wherever the approver actually replies fast. If the director answers WhatsApp in an hour and email in a week, the right design goes through their WhatsApp, not your favorite tool.

fields: Which bank message this piece uses
The case, fact or testimonial it starts from
The generated text, or the link if it's long
idea, draft, review, approved, published, discarded
If it's recycled, which piece it comes from
data.note: The key_message field forces every piece to say something from the approved bank: if you can't fill it in, the piece is filler and it shows. And published/planned per month comes from counting statuses: it's your top metric.

fields: The fact or proof backing it, with date
When to check whether it's still true
data.note: A message with expired evidence is a lawsuit waiting to happen: "92% approve" with three-year-old data becomes misleading advertising. That's why the expires column exists.

fields: yes/no and where the permission is stored
Which pieces it's been used in
data.note: The rule is simple: without archived consent, the social proof doesn't exist for the factory. A great testimonial with no permission is a great problem.

phases.title: Message bank and calendar
phases.goal: Have the approved pantry (messages, data, social proof, tone) and the first four weeks' calendar with owners.
phases.deliverable: The message bank signed off by leadership and the calendar with four weeks of realistic pieces.
done: The bank has messages with evidence and an expiry date, tone with examples and a list of forbidden words
Leadership has approved it in writing, all at once and in full
Social proof has its consent located or has been discarded
The four-week calendar fits the team's real hours

steps.title: Run the brief and accept whatever pace comes out
steps.action: Fill in the starter prompt with your real hours and your real approver. Answer the three questions. Whatever sustainable pace comes out is your law for twelve weeks, even if it looks small.
steps.expect: The minimum sustainable pace with its justification, the list of what not to publish, and the success criterion.
steps.stuck: If pride wants more pieces than came out, remember: twelve weeks keeping a modest pace beats two heroic weeks and an abandoned calendar. You can always scale up later.

steps.title: Build the message bank
steps.where: Claude, and whoever knows the data
steps.action: Use the message bank prompt with your real raw material. Verify every fact with its owner before writing it down. Add tone with two examples (do this, not that) and forbidden words.
steps.expect: A two-to-three-page document: messages with evidence and expiry, tone with examples, sector-specific prohibitions.
steps.stuck: If a message has no evidence, don't throw it out: mark it "pending evidence" and don't use it until you have some. That pending list is also a useful list of things the organization should be measuring.

steps.title: Hunt for social proof with permission
steps.where: Reviews, client emails, and the phone
steps.action: Gather testimonials, cases and figures into the social_proof tab. For each, locate or request consent (a "can we quote your review with your name?" email and its saved reply is enough).
steps.expect: A list of usable social proof, with the consent column marked yes and the permission archived.
steps.stuck: Asking for permission feels like a chore and works better than you'd think: most people happily say yes. A two-line template, ten sends, fifteen minutes.

steps.title: Get leadership's sign-off, once and fully
steps.where: A short meeting with whoever approves
steps.action: Present the whole bank and ask for a sign-off on the entire document, with the deal: what's signed off doesn't get re-approved piece by piece; only sensitive pieces and ones debuting a new message go through you.
steps.expect: The bank approved in writing and the agreed approval circuit: what goes through leadership and what doesn't.
steps.stuck: If leadership wants to keep seeing everything, accept it and note it down: after two weeks of approving eight identical pieces, reality renegotiates the deal better than you can.

phases.title: The draft factory
phases.goal: Turn every calendar row into a draft with the house voice, no blank page.
phases.deliverable: The factory flow working: reads the calendar, drafts with the bank, and leaves pieces ready for review.
done: The flow reads the calendar every morning and drafts what's due
Drafts use messages and facts from the bank, not invented ones
Every piece type has its prompt template tuned with real examples
A full week of pieces has come out of the factory and sits in review status

steps.title: Prepare the calendar for the machine
steps.action: Create the sheet with the data model's columns, closed-list statuses, and four weeks of pieces with key_message and raw_material filled in. No accents or capitals in column names.
steps.expect: Every row with what the AI will need: type, channel, message from the bank and raw material. An incomplete row will produce a generic draft: garbage in, garbage out.
steps.stuck: If you struggle to fill in raw_material for many rows, that's a good signal to read: you don't have a writing problem, you have a pantry problem. Go back to the bank before manufacturing.

steps.title: Import the flow and connect credentials
steps.action: Import this kit's flow. Connect Sheets, Slack, Gmail and the model credential (Header Auth). Put your sheet's ID where it belongs.
steps.expect: The flow imported with green credentials, not yet activated.
steps.stuck: If the Sheets node can't find the tab, check the name matches exactly, capitalization included. It's the number one stumble.

steps.title: Tune the writing prompt with your examples
steps.action: Paste this kit's writing prompt with your bank inside, and add one or two examples of your own pieces that worked (or the tone you want). Run it against three rows of different types.
steps.expect: Three drafts that sound like you, use their row's message and fact, and respect the channel's format.
steps.stuck: If they sound like generic LinkedIn (emojis, "thread", guru phrases), the bank's tone is too vague. Add literal "don't do this" examples: the model learns more from a counterexample than from an adjective.

steps.title: Test the full week dry
steps.action: Run the factory with the entire first week. Check each draft against its row: does it use the message? Is the fact from the bank? Is the length right for the channel? Note failures by pattern, not piece by piece.
steps.expect: A week of drafts in the sheet with draft status, and a short list of patterns to fix in the prompt.
steps.stuck: Fix the prompt once per pattern and regenerate the week. Hand-correcting drafts without touching the prompt condemns you to correcting the same thing every week forever.

steps.title: Turn on the daily rhythm
steps.action: Activate the flow with its morning trigger. From here on, the factory drafts whatever the calendar calls for, and your job starts at review.
steps.expect: Every morning with pieces due, the draft shows up on its own and an alert arrives saying material's waiting for review.
steps.stuck: If a morning generates nothing, check the calendar first (were there rows with today's date and idea status?) and then n8n's executions. 80% of the time it's the calendar, not the machine.

phases.title: Decks and on-brand visual pieces
phases.goal: Produce presentations and graphic pieces from approved scripts, with templates that protect the brand.
phases.deliverable: The master deck built in Gamma or Canva from an approved script, and the brand templates for social pieces.
done: The deck's script was approved as text before anything got laid out
The built deck only uses data and proof from the bank, with the brand consistent
There are locked Canva templates for the two or three usual piece formats
Someone outside the project has seen the deck and understood what's asked and what's offered

steps.title: Write the script for your most-repeated deck
steps.action: With the deck script prompt, write the presentation you need most often (sales, institutional or results): one message line per slide, with its fact from the bank.
steps.expect: An 8-15 slide script where each has a single message and its evidence. Readable in full in two minutes.
steps.stuck: If a slide needs three sentences to explain, that's two slides. And if the whole script doesn't answer "what do we want the viewer to do?", the closing slide is missing, and that's the one that matters.

steps.title: Approve the script before touching Gamma
steps.action: Give the plain-text script to whoever approves. Correct on the text. Only once the text is signed off do you move to layout.
steps.expect: The script approved in writing, with corrections made where they're cheap.
steps.stuck: If the approver says "just build it and I'll see how it looks", explain the deal: fixing text costs minutes; fixing a built deck costs hours. Most understand the first time; the rest understand by the second deck.

steps.title: Build the deck in Gamma and adjust it
steps.action: Paste the approved script into Gamma, pick a sober theme, apply brand colors and generate. Review slide by slide: check the tool hasn't added claims that weren't in the script.
steps.expect: The complete deck, faithful to the script, exported to PDF and to editable PowerPoint.
steps.stuck: Gamma sometimes "enriches" with its own phrases when generating. Compare against the script: anything that wasn't there, gone. The aesthetics are its; the claims are yours.

steps.title: Create the brand templates in Canva
steps.action: Build one template per usual format (post with a fact, tips carousel, date announcement) with fixed colors, fonts and logo. Mark the text boxes that change and don't touch anything else piece by piece.
steps.expect: Two or three templates anyone on the team can fill in ten minutes without breaking the brand.
steps.stuck: If every piece asks for "a bit different", the brand dissolves in three weeks. The template is a decision already made: that's its whole point.

steps.title: Time the whole circuit for one piece
steps.action: Take one calendar row and carry it from idea to published while timing: factory draft, review, visual with template, approval, publishing. Note the time per step.
steps.expect: A real time-per-piece figure (well-set-up: 20-40 person-minutes for a post with visual). It's your number for planning and for defending the system.
steps.stuck: If one step eats up the time, that's your next improvement. A long review usually means weak drafts: go back to the prompt. A long approval, an overloaded approver: review phase 1's deal.

phases.title: Approval, measurement and handover
phases.goal: Sustain the pace for twelve weeks: approve with a log, measure what's published, recycle the best, and be able to hand off the wheel.
phases.deliverable: Four weeks of pieces published with their log, the monthly report, and the operations sheet tested by another person.
done: Four straight weeks with published/planned above 80%
Every published piece has its approval logged with who and when
The first monthly report exists: consistency, what worked, inquiries, cost
Another person has run the circuit for a whole week with the sheet, without you

steps.title: Run the brand review on every piece
steps.where: Claude or the flow itself, plus your judgment
steps.action: Before approving, run every piece through the brand review prompt: facts against the bank, tone, forbidden words, rights and sensitivities. The AI flags; you decide.
steps.expect: Every piece with its review: either clean, or with concrete warnings you fix before approving.
steps.stuck: If the review never finds anything, be suspicious of the checklist, not the pieces: feed it the last two real mistakes that slipped through and see if it catches them.

steps.title: Close the month with the four-figure report
steps.where: Each platform's stats and the sheet
steps.action: With the monthly report prompt: published/planned, the three best-performing pieces and why, attributable inquiries or results, and cost (tools + API + hours). To leadership, in half a page.
steps.expect: Half a page with four numbers and one decision for next month (what piece type comes in, what goes out).
steps.stuck: If you can't attribute inquiries, start asking "how did you hear about us?" on every form and call. Within a month you'll have the data you're missing.

steps.title: Build the recycling routine
steps.action: Pick the month's best piece and plan its derivatives in the calendar with parent_piece filled in: the post that worked becomes a carousel, the success story becomes a deck slide and a newsletter paragraph.
steps.expect: Two or three new calendar rows that don't start from scratch. Month two of the factory costs less than month one: that's the sign it's working.
steps.stuck: Recycling isn't repeating: change the angle or the format, not just the date. If even that feels like too much effort, the piece wasn't that good: check the metrics again.

steps.title: Rehearse the week without you
steps.where: With whoever will replace you, and the sheet in front
steps.action: Write the operations sheet (use the handover prompt, adapting: calendar, factory, review, approval, publishing, report) and have another person run the circuit for a whole week. You just watch.
steps.expect: A week published without your hand in it. The questions they ask are the lines missing from the sheet.
steps.stuck: If there's nobody who can replace you for even a week, the system has a single point of failure with your name on it. That's the risk to raise with leadership, with this rehearsal as evidence.

prompts.name: Build the bank of approved messages
prompts.when: In phase 1, before producing anything. Reviewed every quarter.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a communications strategist for small organizations. We're going to build my organization's message bank: the document with everything we can state, from which every piece of content will come. It's not a creative exercise: it's an inventory with evidence.

My raw material, unpolished:
- Organization and what it offers: [ORGANIZATION]
- Data and figures we have, with date and source: [DATA]
- Testimonials and cases available: [PROOF]
- What really sets us apart according to our clients (not according to us): [DIFFERENCE]
- How we talk: two examples of our own text that sound good and one that sounds bad: [TONE EXAMPLES]
- What's sensitive or forbidden in our sector: [LIMITS]

Build the bank with these exact sections:

1. Key messages: five to eight statements we can make, each with its evidence next to it and a suggested expiry date (when we'll need to check it's still true). If a statement from my raw material has no evidence, put it in a separate "pending evidence: don't use yet" list. Don't dress it up.
2. House tone: three concrete rules deduced from my examples (not adjectives: rules, like "sentences under 15 words" or "always informal"), plus a "do this / not that" list with one example sentence per rule.
3. Forbidden words and promises: what we never write, including our sector's legal limits ([LIMITS]) and the AI tells that give us away ("in an increasingly...", "discover", "unlock").
4. Frequently asked questions from the audience with the one-line official answer, so every piece answers them the same way.
5. The three topics about which we have NOTHING to say yet, so we don't publish filler about them.

Be concise: the whole bank must fit in three pages, because it goes inside every writing prompt. If my raw material is thin in any section, say so clearly and say what to go get instead of padding with generalities.

fill.example: Civil service exam academy with 200 students, in-person and online

fill.what: Real figures with date and source
fill.example: 68% pass rate in 2025 (official listings), 200 current students, 14 years open

fill.what: Testimonials and cases, with or without permission yet
fill.example: 31 Google reviews at 4.8; three placed students willing to go on record with their name

fill.what: What clients say when choosing you
fill.example: "Small groups and the tutor actually picks up the phone": shows up in half the reviews

fill.what: Real texts of yours, two good and one bad, pasted
fill.example: [the post that worked best], [a well-received email], [the post that sounded like a brochure]
Don't promise a spot or a pass, don't cite students without permission, don't compare academies by name

prompts.expect: A three-page bank with evidenced, expiring messages, tone rules with examples, prohibitions, official FAQ, and the topics off-limits for lack of material.
prompts.stuck: If the messages come out as slogans ("quality training centered on the person"), send them back: "every message must contain a checkable fact or it's out". The bank is an inventory of truths, not a brochure.

prompts.name: Write a piece from the calendar
prompts.when: This is the prompt for the factory's writing node. It runs on every row that's due.
prompts.prompt:
You are [ORGANIZATION]'s content writer. You write a piece from the brief below and the message bank. A person will review it before publishing, but write as if it were going out as-is.

The house's message bank (everything statable; what's not here does NOT exist):
[BANK]

The piece's brief:
- Channel: [CHANNEL]
- Type: [TYPE]
- Key message it must convey: [MESSAGE]
- Raw material (the case, fact or testimonial it starts from): [MATERIAL]

Format rules by channel:
[FORMATS]

Hard rules:
- The piece develops the brief's key message and only that one. One piece, one idea.
- Every fact, figure or testimonial comes from the bank or the raw material, literally. If you need one that's not there, write MISSING DATA: and what's missing, and continue.
- Follow the bank's tone rules and forbidden words. Not a single AI tell.
- No promises the bank doesn't back and no unsupported superlatives.
- The first-line hook comes from the raw material (the specific detail, the figure, the testimonial's phrase), not a suspense formula.
- Close with the call to action appropriate to the channel, with a concrete verb.
- If the raw material is thin for this message (no honest angle), say so in one line at the top: WEAK PIECE: and the reason. I'd rather discard a piece than publish filler.

Return only the piece's text, ready to review. If the type is carousel or script, structure it by numbered screens or slides.

fill.example: a civil service exam academy in Murcia

fill.what: The whole message bank, pasted (or its messages, tone and prohibitions sections)
fill.example: Messages: 1) 68% pass rate in 2025 (source: official listings)... Tone: short sentences, informal... Forbidden: promising a spot...
{{ $json.canal }}
{{ $json.tipo }}
{{ $json.mensaje_clave }}
{{ $json.materia_prima }}

fill.what: Your per-channel rules, written once for good

prompts.name: Write a deck's script before laying it out
prompts.when: Every time a presentation is needed, before opening Gamma or Canva.
prompts.prompt:
Act as an executive presentation consultant. We're going to write the SCRIPT for a presentation: what each slide says, in plain text, to approve before laying anything out. Aesthetics come after and aren't yours to decide.

Context:
- Who's presenting and who's the audience: [WHO TO WHOM]
- Objective: what the audience should do or decide by the end: [OBJECTIVE]
- How much time there is to present: [TIME]
- The house's approved message and data bank: [BANK]
- Context of the moment (why now, what they already know, what objections they'll bring): [MOMENT]

Write the script with these rules:

1. One slide, one message. Each slide is defined in three lines: HEADLINE (the sentence that's read, which states something, not a label like "Our Services"), CONTENT (the fact, chart or example backing it, pulled from the bank) and NOTE (what the presenter says that isn't written).
2. Structure: open with the audience's problem or situation (not with who we are), prove it with data and cases from the bank, and close with the concrete ask: what decision, how much money, what next step and when.
3. The number of slides comes from the time: [TIME] divided by roughly two minutes per slide. If the content doesn't fit, cut content, not time per slide.
4. Every fact in the script must exist in the bank. If the argument needs a fact that's not there, write MISSING DATA: on its slide and say how to get it. Don't estimate it.
5. Anticipate this audience's two most likely objections and decide: either answer them on a slide, or leave them ready in NOTE for the Q&A. Tell me which you chose and why.
6. At the end, the minute-by-minute: which slide falls on which minute, for rehearsal.

If the objective I gave you is vague ("present the company"), don't write the script: give me back three concrete objective options and wait for me to choose.

fill.example: The director, in front of the education councilor and two city hall staff

fill.what: The decision or action you're seeking
fill.example: Get them to give us the community center's classroom two afternoons a week next year
15 minutes plus questions

fill.what: The approved messages and data, pasted
fill.example: 200 students, 68% pass rate 2025, 14 years in the neighborhood, 31 reviews at 4.8...

fill.what: Why now and what objections you expect
fill.example: Facility allocations get decided in October; likely objection: "you're a private company"

prompts.expect: An 8-15 slide script with headline-statement, content from the bank and presenter note, objections addressed, and the minute-by-minute.
prompts.stuck: If headlines come out as labels ("About Us", "Services"), ask again: "every headline must be a sentence that states something I want them to remember". The headline-as-statement is half the craft of a good deck.

prompts.name: The brand review before approval

prompts.prompt:
Act as [ORGANIZATION]'s brand and compliance reviewer. I'm giving you a piece ready to publish and the house rules. Your job is to find problems, not give creative opinions or rewrite the style. If you find nothing, say so in one line; don't invent nitpicks to look useful.

House rules:
- Message bank (the only thing statable): [BANK]
- Tone and forbidden words: [TONE AND PROHIBITIONS]
- Sector sensitivities: [SENSITIVITIES]

The piece to review (channel: [CHANNEL]):
[PIECE]

Review in this order and return a table with columns: problem, severity (blocks / fix / suggestion), where it is (quote the exact sentence), proposed fix:

1. Facts: every figure, date, price or factual statement in the piece — is it in the bank or the raw material? Ones that aren't are BLOCKS: point out which and where it should come from.
2. Promises: is there anything promising results, timelines or terms the bank doesn't back? In my sector ([SENSITIVITIES]) this can be misleading advertising: maximum severity.
3. People: does anyone appear by name, photo or recognizable case? If the piece uses social proof, is its consent on record? No archived consent, BLOCKS.
4. Tone: does it break any tone rule or use forbidden words? Quote the sentence and give the alternative.
5. AI tells: flag any phrase that reveals unedited generated text.
6. Timing context: is there anything that could read badly today given current events or notable dates? If you can't know, say "check current events" and what to check.
7. Visual rights: if the piece describes images, where do they come from and do we have the right to use them?

Finish with a one-line verdict: READY, READY WITH CHANGES (which ones) or BLOCKED (why). The final decision belongs to the approver: you inform.

prompts.name: The half-page monthly content report
prompts.when: The last business day of each month, with the stats in front of you.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a pragmatic content analyst. I'm giving you this month's data from my calendar and the platforms, and I want the half-page report for leadership: numbers, honest readings and one decision. No marketing fluff.

Month's data:
- Pieces planned and published, by channel: [PLANNED AND PUBLISHED]
- Metrics per piece (reach, interactions, clicks, whatever each platform has): [METRICS]
- Attributable inquiries, messages or business results (with how they were attributed): [BUSINESS]
- Month's cost: tools, API and person-hours: [COST]
- What happened outside the normal (campaigns, holidays, a controversial piece): [CONTEXT]

Give me, in this order and in half a page total:

1. The consistency figure: published over planned, compared to last month. It's the report's first line because it's the metric that predicts all the others.
2. The three best-performing pieces, with a hypothesis for why (format, topic, hook, day) marked as a hypothesis, not a certainty. And the worst, with the same honesty.
3. The business figure: what came in attributable to content, and what part of the funnel is still in the dark.
4. Cost per published piece, everything included.
5. ONE decision for next month, deduced from the above: a piece type coming in or out, a schedule change, a specific experiment with its success criterion. Just one: if you propose five changes, I won't know which one worked.

Rules: if a metric can't support a conclusion (small sample, odd month), say so instead of forcing a reading. Don't use "engagement" without translating it into concrete interactions. And if consistency dropped below 80%, that's the default decision for the month: fix the bottleneck before optimizing anything.

fill.what: Per-piece figures, pasted from the platforms

prompts.stuck: If the report grows past half a page, cut from the bottom: leadership reads the first figure and the decision. Everything else is for you.

prompts.name: Write the machine's operations sheet

prompts.prompt:
Write the operations sheet for a content and presentations system, for an organized person who didn't build it. Maximum two pages. Goal: they can run the circuit for a whole week without calling anyone.

System data:
- What it produces and at what pace: [WHAT AND PACE]
- The calendar: where it is and how to fill in a new row: [CALENDAR]
- The factory: what it does on its own each morning and where to see it: [FACTORY]
- The message bank: where it is and when it gets touched: [BANK]
- Review and approval: who, where, with what list: [APPROVAL]
- Publishing: how each channel gets published, with clicks: [PUBLISHING]
- Visual templates: where they are and what can be changed: [TEMPLATES]
- Keys and access: [ACCESS]

The sheet has these sections and no others:

1. A typical week, day by day: what happens on its own, what you do, and how long each task takes. This is the main section: the person should be able to print it and follow it.
2. How a piece gets made start to finish: filling in the row (which fields are essential and why), waiting for the draft, reviewing it with the checklist, building it in the template, requesting approval, publishing and marking the status.
3. The rules that never get skipped, with their reason on the same line: nothing publishes without a logged approval; no fact outside the bank; no recognizable person without archived consent; changes to the bank are approved by leadership.
4. What to do if the factory generates nothing one morning: the three places to check, in order (the calendar, n8n's executions, the credentials), with exact screenshots or paths.
5. The five most likely problems in a table: sign, usual cause, what to do, who to alert if it's not fixed within an hour.
6. What NOT to touch: the node prompts, the locked templates and the active flow, without talking to whoever maintains them.
7. Month close: how the report is made (which prompt, with what data) and who it's sent to.

Informal tone, short sentences, every instruction with its clicks. Think of someone doing this for the first time on a Monday at 9am with little coffee in them.

legal: Undisclosed advertising and claims: what you publish as an organization is commercial communication. Claims about results ("68% pass rate") must be true and demonstrable at the time of publishing: that's why the bank requires evidence and an expiry date on every message.

Testimonials and people's likeness: using a client or student's name, face or words requires their consent, and if they're a minor, their guardians'. Consent gets archived alongside the social proof; without it on file, it doesn't get used.

Image and music rights: Canva-style libraries have license terms (some assets are paid-plan only, others aren't cleared for advertising). Check the resource's license before using it in commercial pieces.
AI-generated content: you're responsible for what you publish, whoever wrote it. The brand review isn't a nice-to-have in the circuit: it's your editorial-responsibility control.
Plagiarism and inspiration: AI can produce text very close to existing sources. If a piece sounds too polished and very specific without your own raw material, check it before publishing.

Regulated sectors (education, health, finance, gambling): they have their own advertising rules. The bank's prohibitions must capture them; if you work for a client in one of these sectors, have their compliance person validate them.

Newsletter and personal data: the mailing list is data processing that needs demonstrable consent, information at signup and an easy unsubscribe on every send. Don't import contacts "we already had" without a basis for it.

Account ownership: social accounts, Canva and templates, in the organization's name with two-person access. An Instagram account on someone's personal phone is the modern equivalent of the domain registered in the brother-in-law's name.
Labeling synthetic content: if you generate images or videos of people or events that look real, label them as generated. European regulation is heading that way, and so is your audience's trust.
This is practical guidance, not legal advice. Campaigns with prizes, comparisons with competitors or regulated sectors: get professional review before publishing.

risks.risk: The calendar gets abandoned by week three
risks.sign: Published/planned below 50%; the last row touched is from ten days ago
risks.fix: The pace came out too ambitious: cut it in half and keep it. Modest consistency beats intermittent ambition. That's why consistency is the top metric.

risks.sign: Tells ("in a world where...", rocket emojis), pieces interchangeable with any competitor's
risks.fix: The bank with literal "don't do this" examples inside the prompt, and the brand review catching tells. If it persists, the bank is vague: rewrite it with your own real texts.

risks.risk: An old or false fact gets published
risks.sign: A figure in a piece that isn't in the bank, or is there but with expired evidence
risks.fix: The MISSING DATA rule in the prompt, the bank's expires column reviewed quarterly, and fact-checking as the first item on the review list. All three layers.

risks.sign: Pieces sitting in review for three days; things publish late or without approval "just this once"
risks.fix: The phase 1 deal: the signed-off bank exempts pieces that don't debut a new message from piece-by-piece approval. And a named backup approver.

risks.risk: A testimonial with no permission makes it into a piece
risks.sign: A face or name published with the consent column empty or set to no
risks.fix: The hard rule: without archived consent, social proof doesn't exist for the factory. And the brand review checks it piece by piece.

risks.risk: The deck gets laid out before the script is approved
risks.sign: Three versions of the built deck circulating with different content; hours of layout wasted
risks.fix: Phase 3's discipline: the script gets approved as text. Whoever asks to "just build it and we'll see" pays for the demonstration: show them last time's hours.

risks.risk: Something expensive gets published in the heat of the moment
risks.sign: A piece reacting to current events, published without review because "we had to be there"
risks.fix: Written rule: reactive content goes through the same review, and if there's no time to review, it doesn't publish. No trend gives back the trust a mistake burns.

risks.risk: The machine publishes and nobody measures
risks.sign: Three months of pieces and no report; nobody knows what worked
risks.fix: The half-page monthly report with a date on the calendar, like one more piece. Without measurement, the factory optimizes toward nothing.

defend.question: Won't people notice it's AI-written?
defend.answer: They notice generic text, and rightly so. That's why this system's AI doesn't invent: it writes from our message bank (our data, our cases, tone defined with our own examples), and every piece goes through a review that specifically catches tells and canned tone. The honest test: show three pieces from the system alongside three old ones and let them guess. What they'll notice is that now we publish every week.

defend.question: What if it publishes something incorrect or that puts us at risk?
defend.answer: It can't: the machine doesn't publish. It writes drafts that go through a fact-check against the bank (everything statable has evidence and an expiry date) and a logged approval with name and time before a person publishes it. And if something still slips through, the log says which version went out, who approved it and when: it gets fixed and the lesson gets added to the review.

defend.question: How much real time does this save?
defend.answer: It's timed, not estimated: one piece with a visual went from [X] to [Y] person-minutes, because writing from scratch became reviewing a decent draft. At [n] pieces a month that's [n] hours. The deck that used to take a whole night is now a one-hour script plus Gamma's layout. The phase 3 stopwatch numbers are in the report.

defend.question: Why so few pieces? Competitors post daily.
defend.answer: Because the pace came from our real hours, not from wishful thinking. Twelve weeks keeping three pieces beats two weeks posting daily and a month of silence: consistency is what platforms and audiences reward. The system scales: once the current pace has held at 80% for two months, we add one piece and measure.

defend.question: What about testimonials and photos of people?
defend.answer: No recognizable person appears in a piece without their consent on file: there's a social proof table where every testimonial has its permission archived, and the review checks it piece by piece. With minors, guardian permission or they don't appear. It's one of the rules that never gets skipped, not even in a rush.

defend.question: Does this depend on you forever?
defend.answer: No: there's a two-page operations sheet and a team member already ran the circuit for a whole week without me, as a rehearsal. What stays with me (if you want) is tuning the prompt, the quarterly bank review, and special decks. Daily operation is yours, and it's proven.

words: editorial calendar
The sheet that says which piece goes out, when, where and who's handling it. In this system, it runs everything else.
message bank
The document with what the organization can state: messages with evidence, tone and prohibitions. The factory's pantry.
raw material
The real case, fact, testimonial or experience a piece starts from. Without raw material, AI can only produce filler.
piece
Any publishable unit: a post, a carousel, an article, a deck script.
social proof
Testimonials, cases, figures and logos that prove what you say is true. Only count with archived consent.
deck script
The presentation's text (headline, content and note per slide) approved before laying out. Fixing text is cheap; fixing slides is expensive.
headline-statement
A slide title that states something ("68% passed in 2025"), not a label ("Results"). Audiences remember statements.
consistency
Pieces published over planned. This kit's top metric: it predicts all the others.
AI tell
The phrases that give away unedited generated text: "in an increasingly...", "discover", "don't miss out". They go on the forbidden list.
recycling
Turning a piece that worked into other formats: the talk into clips, the case into a carousel and a slide. The cheapest content is the kind you already paid for.
